issue: Source: "a direct tax, to a certain extent, on the post office". Candidate: "a direct tax of a certain kind on the post office" changes extent into kind.
replacement: Surely no weight will be put on the TITLE here, since changing it could never be taken as using a power that was not granted. ALTERATIONS in the body of the document are expressly authorized, and so are NEW PROVISIONS in it. So the Convention had power to change the title, to add new articles and to alter old ones. Must we then admit that the power was overstepped as long as some of the old articles survive? Anyone who says so should at least draw the line between authorized and usurped innovations. He should show what degree of change falls within ALTERATIONS AND FURTHER PROVISIONS and what degree amounts to a TRANSMUTATION of the government. Will it be said that the alterations should not have touched the substance of the Confederation? The States would never have appointed a convention so solemnly, or described its objects so broadly, if they had not contemplated some SUBSTANTIAL reform. Will it be said that the FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES of the Confederation lay outside the Convention's purview and should not have been changed? I ask, What are these principles? Do they require that the States be treated, in establishing the Constitution, as distinct and independent sovereigns? The proposed Constitution treats them that way. Do they require that the members of the government be appointed by the legislatures and not by the people of the States? One branch of the new government is to be appointed by these legislatures; and under the Confederation the delegates to Congress MAY ALL be appointed directly by the people, and in two States(1) they actually are. Do they require that the government's powers act on the States and not directly on individuals? In some cases, as has been shown, the powers of the new government will act on the States in their collective characters. In some cases, too, the powers of the existing government act directly on individuals. Take cases of capture; of piracy; of the post office; of coins, weights and measures; of trade with the Indians; of claims under grants of land by different States; and above all, of trials by courts-martial in the army and navy, where death may be inflicted without a jury or even a civil magistrate. In all these cases the powers of the Confederation operate directly on the persons and interests of individual citizens. Do these fundamental principles require, in particular, that no tax be levied except through the States as intermediaries? The Confederation itself authorizes a direct tax, to a certain extent, on the post office. Congress has also read the power of coinage as allowing it to draw a tribute directly from that source. But leave these instances aside. Was it not an acknowledged aim of the Convention, and the universal expectation of the people, that the regulation of trade should be placed with the general government in a form that would make it a direct source of general revenue? Had Congress not repeatedly recommended this measure as consistent with the fundamental principles of the Confederation? Had not every State but one, New York herself included, gone far enough along with Congress's plan to accept the PRINCIPLE of the innovation? Finally, do these principles require that the powers of the general government be limited, and that beyond that limit the States keep their sovereignty and independence? We have seen that in the new government, as in the old, the general powers are limited, and that in all cases not listed the States keep their sovereign and independent jurisdiction.

issue: Emphasis capital lost: source "the LIBERTY ASSUMED by a VERY FEW deputies" (candidate "take the LIBERTY of recommending", ASSUMED gone). Also source "since it is impossible for the people spontaneously and universally to move in concert" lost its connective "since" (candidate starts a new sentence "The people cannot move..."), and "nominal and nugatory" became the ungrammatical-sounding "a mere name and worthless".
replacement: Consider the position the Convention was in. We can gather from its proceedings that the members were deeply and unanimously impressed by the crisis, which had led their country, almost with one voice, to try so unusual and solemn an experiment: correcting the errors of the very system that had produced the crisis. They were just as deeply and unanimously convinced that a reform like the one they have proposed was absolutely necessary to accomplish the purposes of their appointment. They could not have been ignorant that the great body of citizens throughout this great empire were waiting with the keenest anxiety for the outcome of their deliberations. They had every reason to believe that the opposite feelings stirred the minds and hearts of every foe, foreign and domestic, of the liberty and prosperity of the United States. They had seen, from the beginning and through the course of the experiment, how readily the PROPOSITION of a single State (Virginia), for a partial amendment of the Confederation, had been taken up and advanced. They had seen the LIBERTY ASSUMED by a VERY FEW deputies from a VERY FEW States, meeting at Annapolis, of recommending a great and critical object that was wholly foreign to their commission, not only justified by public opinion but actually carried out by twelve of the thirteen States. They had seen Congress, many times, take on not only recommendatory but operative powers, and the public approve, on occasions and for objects infinitely less urgent than those that were to govern their own conduct. They must have reflected that in every great change of an established government, forms ought to yield to substance. Rigid adherence to forms in such cases would make the transcendent and precious right of the people to "abolish or alter their governments as to them shall seem most likely to effect their safety and happiness"(2) merely nominal and worthless, since the people cannot move toward their goal spontaneously and all together; and it is therefore essential that such changes be started by some INFORMAL AND UNAUTHORIZED PROPOSITIONS from some patriotic and respectable citizen or group of citizens. They must have recalled that it was through this irregular and self-assumed privilege of proposing to the people plans for their safety and happiness that the States were first united against the danger their ancient government threatened; that committees and congresses were formed to concentrate their efforts and defend their rights; and that CONVENTIONS were ELECTED in THE SEVERAL STATES to establish the constitutions under which they are now governed. Nor could they have forgotten that nobody showed petty, ill-timed scruples or zeal for ordinary forms, except those who wished to hide behind these masks their secret hostility to the substance being fought for. They must have kept in mind that, because the plan they framed and proposed was to be submitted TO THE PEOPLE THEMSELVES, this supreme authority's disapproval would destroy it forever, while its approval would wipe out all earlier errors and irregularities. It might even have occurred to them that, where people are inclined to find fault, neglecting to use the full power vested in them, and still more recommending any measure that their commission did not warrant, would draw as much criticism as recommending, at one stroke, a measure fully equal to the national exigencies.

issue: Source is passive: "The answer to these questions has been too far anticipated in another place". Candidate "I have already anticipated the answer ... elsewhere" attributes the earlier discussion to the present writer (Madison), a changed referent.
replacement: The answer to these questions has already been anticipated elsewhere, too fully to allow a lengthy discussion of them here. The answer in fact seems so obvious and conclusive that it hardly justifies a lengthy discussion anywhere. How can anyone decently limit the force needed for defense, when he cannot limit the force of offense? If a federal Constitution could put chains on the ambition of all other nations, or set bounds to their exertions, then it might wisely chain its own government's discretion and set bounds to its exertions for its own safety.

issue: Source "a [resource] which may be inauspicious to its liberties" (unfavorable). Candidate "ominous to its liberties" shifts the sense to foreboding. Also "it deserves praiseworthy caution and precaution" is awkward for "an object of laudable circumspection and precaution".
replacement: It is just as true, though, that the liberties of Rome became in the end the victim of her military triumphs, and that the liberties of Europe, as far as they ever existed, have with few exceptions been the price paid for her military establishments. A standing force is therefore a dangerous provision, even if it is also a necessary one. On the smallest scale it has its drawbacks. On a large scale its consequences may be fatal. On any scale it is an object of laudable caution and precaution. A wise nation will weigh all these considerations. It will not rashly cut itself off from any resource that may prove essential to its safety, but it will bring all its prudence to bear on lessening both the need to resort to a resource that may be unfavorable to its liberties and the danger of doing so.

issue: Source is passive: "It was remarked, on a former occasion". Candidate "I remarked on an earlier occasion" makes the present writer the speaker (the earlier remark is in another paper). NIT: "A generous further share of evils" for "A plentiful addition of evils" reads oddly.
replacement: The proposed Constitution bears the clearest marks of this prudence. The Union itself, which it joins firmly together and secures, removes every pretext for a military establishment that could be dangerous. America united, with a handful of troops or not a single soldier, presents a more forbidding face to foreign ambition than America disunited with a hundred thousand veterans ready to fight. It was remarked on an earlier occasion that the absence of this pretext saved the liberties of one nation in Europe. Because her island position and her naval resources made her safe from the armies of her neighbors, the rulers of Great Britain have never been able, with real or invented dangers, to trick the public into a large peacetime establishment. The distance of the United States from the powerful nations of the world gives them the same happy security. A dangerous establishment can never be either necessary or plausible as long as they remain a united people. But they must never forget, even for a moment, that they owe this advantage to the Union alone. The day it dissolves will be the start of a new order of things. The fears of the weaker States, or the ambition of the stronger States or Confederacies, will set the same example in the New World that Charles VII set in the Old. The example will be followed here for the same reasons that made everyone imitate it there. Instead of drawing from our situation the precious advantage Great Britain draws from hers, America will look just like the continent of Europe. It will show liberty crushed everywhere between standing armies and perpetual taxes. The fortunes of a disunited America will be even more disastrous than Europe's. In Europe the sources of evil are confined within her own borders. No superior powers from another quarter of the globe intrigue among her rival nations, inflame their mutual animosities and turn them into instruments of foreign ambition, jealousy and revenge. In America, the miseries springing from her internal jealousies, contentions and wars would make up only part of her lot. A large additional share of evils would come from the relation in which Europe stands to this quarter of the earth, a relation no other quarter of the earth has to Europe.

issue: Constitutional key term: source "among the several States" (Commerce Clause wording, paraphrased list item). Candidate "among the individual States" per the fixed-term table; the key-term rule for paraphrases of the text suggests keeping "several". Optional.
replacement: The particular restraints placed on the authority of the States, and certain powers of the judicial department, might be included under this head. But the former are set aside for a class of their own, and the latter will be examined in detail when we come to the structure and organization of the government. I will limit myself to a quick review of the remaining powers that fall under this third description. They are: to regulate commerce among the several States and the Indian tribes; to coin money, and to regulate its value and the value of foreign coin; to provide for the punishment of counterfeiting the current coin and securities of the United States; to fix the standard of weights and measures; to establish a uniform rule of naturalization and uniform laws of bankruptcy; to prescribe how the public acts, records and judicial proceedings of each State shall be proved, and what effect they shall have in other States; and to establish post offices and post roads.

issue: Modal strength: source "not improbably terminate in serious interruptions"; candidate "quite likely end" is stronger.
replacement: The existing Confederacy's lack of power to regulate commerce among its members is one of the defects that experience has clearly exposed. To the proofs and remarks that earlier papers have offered on this subject we can add that, without this supplementary provision, the great and essential power of regulating foreign commerce would have been incomplete and ineffective. One very important aim of this power was to relieve the States that import and export through other States from the improper contributions those other States levy on them. If the latter were free to regulate trade between one State and another, we must foresee that they would find ways to burden articles of import and export, while passing through their territory, with duties that would fall on the producers of the exports and the consumers of the imports. Past experience assures us that such a practice would be brought in by future schemes. Both that experience and common knowledge of human affairs assure us that it would feed endless animosities and might well end in serious breaches of the public peace. For those who do not look at the question through passion or self-interest, the desire of the commercial States to collect, in any form, an indirect revenue from their uncommercial neighbors must seem as unwise as it is unfair, because resentment as well as interest would drive the injured party to look for less convenient channels for its foreign trade. But the mild voice of reason, pleading for a broader and lasting interest, is all too often drowned out, in public bodies as well as in individuals, by the clamor of an impatient greed for immediate and excessive gain.

issue: Dropped qualifier. Source: "so that it may be in the power of a particular State, or rather every State is laid under a necessity, not only to confer ...". Candidate: "So a particular State, or rather every State, is placed under a necessity" drops "it may be in the power of".
replacement: The differences among the States in the rules of naturalization have long been noted as a fault in our system, and as a basis for intricate and delicate questions. The fourth article of the Confederation declares "that the FREE INHABITANTS of each of these States, paupers, vagabonds, and fugitives from justice, excepted, shall be entitled to all privileges and immunities of FREE CITIZENS in the several States; and THE PEOPLE of each State shall, in every other, enjoy all the privileges of trade and commerce," etc. The language here is remarkably confused. It is hard to tell why the terms FREE INHABITANTS are used in one part of the article, FREE CITIZENS in another and PEOPLE in another, or what was meant by adding "all the privileges of trade and commerce" to "all privileges and immunities of free citizens." It seems nearly unavoidable, though, to conclude that those who count as FREE INHABITANTS of a State, even if not citizens of that State, are entitled in every other State to all the privileges of FREE CITIZENS of that other State. That means greater privileges than they may have in their own State. So it may be in the power of a particular State, or rather every State is placed under a necessity, of conferring the rights of citizenship in other States, not only on anyone it admits to such rights within itself, but on anyone it allows to become an inhabitant within its jurisdiction. But suppose we accepted an interpretation of the term "inhabitants" that confined the promised privileges to citizens alone. The difficulty would only be reduced, not removed. Each State would still keep the very improper power of naturalizing aliens in every other State. In one State a short residence confers all the rights of citizenship, and in another more important qualifications are required. So an alien who is legally barred from certain rights in the latter State may get around the bar merely by having lived earlier in the former. In this way the law of one State is absurdly made to override the law of another within that other State's own jurisdiction. We owe it to mere chance that we have so far escaped very serious embarrassments over this. By the laws of several States, certain kinds of aliens who had made themselves obnoxious were put under prohibitions that were inconsistent not only with the rights of citizenship but with the privilege of residence. What would have followed if such persons, by residence or otherwise, had acquired the character of citizens under the laws of another State, and had then claimed their rights as citizens, both to residence and to citizenship, in the State that had banned them? Whatever the legal consequences might have been, other consequences would probably have followed that were too serious not to be guarded against. The new Constitution has accordingly, and very properly, made provision against them, and against all other consequences of the Confederation's defect on this point, by authorizing the general government to establish a uniform rule of naturalization throughout the United States.

issue: Modal strength: source "If the interposition of the general government should not be needed" (hypothetical). Candidate "If the general government never needs to step in" is a universal claim. Also dropped qualifier: source "It may possibly be asked".
replacement: In a confederacy founded on republican principles and made up of republican members, the superintending government clearly ought to have authority to defend the system against aristocratic or monarchical innovations. The closer such a union is, the more interest the members have in one another's political institutions, and the greater their right to insist that the forms of government under which they entered the compact be SUBSTANTIALLY kept. But a right implies a remedy; and where else could the remedy be placed than where the Constitution places it? Governments of unlike principles and forms have proved less suited to any sort of federal coalition than governments of a similar nature. "As the confederate republic of Germany," says Montesquieu, "consists of free cities and petty states, subject to different princes, experience shows us that it is more imperfect than that of Holland and Switzerland." "Greece was undone," he adds, "as soon as the king of Macedon obtained a seat among the Amphictyons." In the latter case, no doubt, the new member's disproportionate strength, as well as its monarchical form, had a share in bringing about the events. It may possibly be asked what need there could be for such a precaution, and whether it might become a pretext for altering the State governments without the States' own agreement. These questions have ready answers. If the interposition of the general government should not be needed, the provision for such an event will be only a harmless superfluity in the Constitution. But who can say what experiments the caprice of particular States, the ambition of enterprising leaders, or the intrigues and influence of foreign powers may produce? To the second question, the answer is that if the general government steps in under this constitutional authority, it will of course be bound to stay within the authority. But the authority reaches no further than a GUARANTY of a republican form of government, which assumes that a government of the form to be guaranteed already exists. So as long as the States keep their existing republican forms, the federal Constitution guarantees them. Whenever the States choose to put other republican forms in their place, they have a right to do so and to claim the federal guaranty for the new ones. The only restriction on them is that they may not exchange republican for antirepublican Constitutions, a restriction that, it is presumed, will hardly be thought a grievance.

issue: "magistracy" for a county-level authority may read as judges to a modern reader (STYLE-NOTE magistrate rule).
replacement: At first glance it might seem not to fit republican theory to suppose either that a majority lacks the right to overthrow a government or that a minority will have the force to do so; and so it might seem that federal interposition could never be required except when it would be improper. But theoretical reasoning, here as in most other cases, has to be qualified by what practice teaches. Why could illicit combinations for violent purposes not be formed by a majority of a State, especially a small State, just as they could by a majority of a county or district within the same State? And if the State's authority ought to protect the local officials in the second case, ought not the federal authority to support the State authority in the first? Besides, some parts of the State constitutions are so interwoven with the federal Constitution that a violent blow to one cannot be struck without wounding the other. Insurrections in a State will rarely lead to federal interposition unless the number involved bears some proportion to the friends of government. It will be far better for the superintending power to put down the violence in such cases than for the majority to be left to defend its cause in a bloody and stubborn contest. The existence of a right to interpose will generally spare the need to use it.
